passage:
Last Diwali I touched Periamma's feet in about half a second, phone still in my other hand, already turning away. She blessed me anyway. Later my friend Francis, who'd come over for sweets, asked, 'What does it mean when you do that?' I started to say 'respect', and stopped. It hadn't meant anything. It was a habit, like wiping my shoes on the mat.
This year I tried it differently. I put the phone down, bent properly, and looked at Periamma's face when she touched my head. Her hand trembled a little. She said my name twice. I don't know if it counts as real yet, but I was actually there.
Nirmala

qa.q: What was in Nirmala's other hand last Diwali?
qa.a: The phone.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel after Francis's question?
qa.a: Nirmala felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising the gesture had become an empty habit.

qa.q: What changed in how Nirmala touched Periamma's feet this year, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Nirmala put the phone down, bent properly and looked at Periamma, so the gesture carried real attention to the person instead of show.

qa.q: How might Periamma have felt this year when Nirmala bowed slowly?
qa.a: Periamma likely felt truly seen and moved, which may be why her hand trembled and she said Nirmala's name twice.

grounding: Shows a teenager who realises touching feet had become a hurried habit and makes it meaningful by doing it with attention to the person.

passage:
Coach's notebook, Sunday. Harish, under-16 squad.
Before the final, Vikas lined up with the others to touch my feet, as the boys all do. He did it at a run, eyes on the scoreboard, gone before my hand reached his head. Afterwards he asked, 'Sir, does it even mean anything, or is it just for luck?' Honest question. I told him I'd rather have one real thank-you a season than a rushed bow every match.
Today, packing up, he stopped, bent slowly and said, 'Thanks for the extra nets, Sir.' Then he looked me in the eye. That one counted. I'll tell the squad the bow is optional; the attention isn't.

qa.q: What did Vikas thank Harish for?
qa.a: The extra nets.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he asked if the bow means anything?
qa.a: Vikas felt unsure and a bit uneasy, suspecting the rushed bow had become a habit or a luck charm rather than real respect.

qa.q: What was wise about Harish's reply to Vikas?
qa.a: Harish welcomed the honest question and pointed to attention and real thanks, which gave the bow meaning instead of demanding it.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Vikas bent slowly and looked him in the eye?
qa.a: Harish felt truly respected and touched; that one bow counted more than all the rushed ones.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who questions whether touching feet is respect or habit after doing it hurriedly, and finds it becomes real when done with attention to the person.

passage:
"Bye, Dadaji!" Vandana tapped his knee on her way out, not even bending properly, bag already on her shoulder.
Her father, Kamal, caught her at the door. "What was that?"
"I touched his feet."
"You touched his knee. In passing. Like a doorbell."
"Papa, honestly, isn't it just a habit? Does Dadaji even care?"
"Go and look at him."
Vandana turned. Dadaji was still sitting with his hand half-raised for the blessing she hadn't waited for.
Her throat tightened. She went back, knelt properly, and waited. His hand came down on her head, warm and a little shaky. "Do well in the exam, bitiya."
"I will, Dadaji." This time she looked at his face.

qa.q: What did Vandana actually touch on her way out?
qa.a: Vandana touched his knee, in passing.

qa.q: What did Vandana feel when she saw Dadaji's hand half-raised?
qa.a: Vandana felt a pang of guilt and tenderness; her throat tightened at the blessing she hadn't waited for.

qa.q: What made the second touch real?
qa.a: She went back, knelt properly, waited for his blessing and looked at his face, paying attention to him instead of rushing.

qa.q: What was it like for Dadaji when Vandana tapped his knee and left?
qa.a: Dadaji was left with his hand half-raised, probably feeling a little overlooked, until she came back.

grounding: Shows a teenager who touches a grandparent's feet in a hurry, questions whether it is habit, and finds it becomes real when done with attention.

passage:
I'm Salma, and I still feel a bit silly about my first visit to Yogesh's house.

Everyone there touched his Aaji's feet when they came in. Yogesh did it in half a second, already asking about lunch. I panicked and copied him, a quick dip, fingers nowhere near her feet. Aaji smiled politely. I felt like a fraud.

On the bus home I wondered whether it was respect or just habit for him too. It had certainly been a show for me.

The next time, I said "Assalamu alaikum, Aaji," the way I greet my own grandmother, and sat beside her. She showed me her old wedding photos for an hour. Yogesh got bored and left.

When I stood to go, Aaji held my hand for a long moment. That felt like more respect than any bow.

qa.q: What did Aaji show Salma on the second visit?
qa.a: Aaji showed her old wedding photos for an hour.

qa.q: What did Salma feel after copying the quick dip?
qa.a: Salma felt embarrassed and like a fraud, since the gesture had only been for show.

qa.q: Which choice showed real respect, and why?
qa.a: Greeting Aaji in Salma's own way and sitting with her for an hour; attention to her as a person made it real.

qa.q: How might Aaji have felt when Salma sat with her?
qa.a: Aaji likely felt valued and enjoyed the company, which is why she held Salma's hand for a long moment.

grounding: Shows a teenager who makes a hurried gesture for show, wonders whether it is respect or habit, and finds that attention to the person is what makes respect real.

passage:
Coach's note, district kabaddi camp, day 4

Before practice the players line up to touch my feet. Most do it in a rush. Akash does it slowly only when the selectors are watching.

Today Farida, fifteen, stayed back. "Coach, is it real respect or just habit? Akash does it for show. And I'm not sure I should do it at all."

I told her the truth: I don't need anyone's forehead near my shoes. What I notice is who listens, who helps the juniors, who looks me in the eye.

What I did next: from tomorrow, anyone who wants to touch feet can, but slowly, looking up, and saying one thing they'll work on. A handshake with the same words counts just as much. Akash looked lost. Farida went first, with a handshake.

qa.q: When does Akash touch feet slowly?
qa.a: Akash does it slowly only when the selectors are watching.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she stayed back to ask?
qa.a: Farida felt unsure and uneasy, doubting the gesture meant anything when Akash did it for show.

qa.q: How does the coach's new routine give the greeting meaning?
qa.a: Whether touching feet or shaking hands, each player must slow down, look up and name one thing to work on, so attention replaces show.

qa.q: How might Akash feel about the new routine?
qa.a: Akash looked lost, perhaps uneasy that the show no longer works when everyone must mean it.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning whether a greeting done hurriedly or for show is real respect, and a coach making attention the point.

passage:
Diwali night
Today I touched about fifteen people's feet. Honestly, most of them I did in two seconds, half-bent, eyes on my phone, because the cousins were waiting to burst crackers. Nani caught my hand after I did hers. "Are you touching my feet or the floor?" Everyone laughed. I laughed too, but I felt a bit ashamed.
Later I was texting Ayesha. She asked what touching feet actually means, because her family says salaam instead. I started typing "respect" and then stopped. If it's respect, why was I doing it like ticking boxes?
So after the crackers I went back to Nani, who was sitting alone with her tea. I touched her feet slowly this time, and looked at her face. She put her hand on my head for a long time and didn't say anything. Her eyes were wet. It felt completely different. I think it's only real when you actually see the person.
Yash

qa.q: What did Nani ask Yash?
qa.a: "Are you touching my feet or the floor?"

qa.q: How did Yash feel when Nani caught the hurried gesture?
qa.a: Yash felt a bit ashamed, even while laughing with everyone.

qa.q: What made the second time real?
qa.a: Doing it slowly and looking at Nani's face gave the gesture real attention, so it became respect rather than a ticked box.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt the second time?
qa.a: She probably felt deeply touched and loved, keeping her hand on Yash's head with wet eyes.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who questions whether touching feet is respect or habit, and finds it real when done with attention.
